notes.front: In lean, what counts as waste?
notes.back: Any activity that does not directly help make the product or service the customer wants, at the time they want it.
notes.explanation: The guide describes lean as a set of principles and methods aimed at finding and removing this non-value-added activity.
notes.example: Like a finished permit that sits in a tray for a week: the wait adds nothing the customer wants.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “What is Lean Manufacturing?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is DOWNTIME in lean?
notes.back: A memory aid for the eight common process wastes that lean targets, one letter per waste.
notes.explanation: The Starter Kit pairs each letter with office examples, such as errors in documents or waiting for approvals.
notes.example: Like a mnemonic for a pre-flight checklist, but each letter names a kind of waste to look for.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is 5S?
notes.back: A systematic five-step method for making a workspace clean and orderly, and keeping it that way.
notes.explanation: The guide calls it the usual starting point for changing a shop floor, and a foundation for more advanced lean methods.
notes.example: Like clearing out and labelling a shared kitchen, then keeping a rota so it stays tidy.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “5S”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is value stream mapping (VSM)?
notes.back: Drawing a high-level visual picture of the activities that deliver a product or service to customers.
notes.explanation: Those activities together are the value stream; practitioners use the map to find major sources of non-value-added time.
notes.example: Like tracing a parcel’s whole journey from order to doorstep, noting every place it sits waiting.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does kaizen mean in lean?
notes.back: Continual improvement: small, incremental changes, applied routinely and sustained over a long time, that add up to large gains.
notes.explanation: The guide says lean production is founded on this idea, and explains kaizen as two Japanese words meaning ‘to take apart’ and ‘to make good’. LeanOhio simply translates it as ‘improvement’ or ‘change for the better’.
notes.example: Like trimming a minute off a daily routine each week until, a year later, it is far quicker.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Kaizen Events”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a kaizen event?
notes.back: A short, intensive improvement event in which people from several functions and levels quickly improve one targeted process.
notes.explanation: The guide says lean is usually put into practice through such events, which also help build a culture of continual improvement.
notes.example: Like a renovation weekend for one room, rather than slowly redecorating the whole house over years.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Kaizen Events”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is just-in-time (JIT) production?
notes.back: Making the products customers want, when they want them, in the amount they want.
notes.explanation: Conventional mass production makes large runs and stores them until ordered; this approach cuts inventory and work in process instead.
notes.example: Like a sandwich shop that makes each sandwich once it is ordered, rather than filling a fridge every morning.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a kanban?
notes.back: A signal, used in a pull system, that production should start; it can be a card, board, light or bin, among other forms.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio gives the word as Japanese for signal: the next step uses it to ask for more work from the step before.
notes.example: Like an empty milk bottle left on the doorstep, telling the milkman to bring another.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Kanban”, p. 7
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is takt time?
notes.back: The rate at which each product must be completed to meet customer needs, expressed as time per part.
notes.explanation: The guidance calls it critical to the daily scheduling that levelled production needs.
notes.example: Like a bakery that must finish a loaf every two minutes to keep up with the day’s orders.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Little’s law state?
notes.back: The average number of items in a process equals the average rate items leave it times the average time each spends in it.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam presents it as an equation that can be used to balance capacity with demand.
notes.example: Like a café queue: if two people leave each minute and each stays five minutes, about ten are inside at once.
notes.source: MoreSteam, Little’s Law Calculator Tutorial
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is one-piece flow?
notes.back: Moving products through a process one piece at a time, rather than processing many parts before passing them on.
notes.explanation: The guidance says the approach aims to cut the time a single product takes to flow through the whole production process.
notes.example: Like washing, drying and putting away each plate in turn, instead of washing the whole stack first.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – Cellular Manufacturing, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is cellular manufacturing?
notes.back: Arranging work stations and equipment in sequence so materials flow smoothly through production with minimal transport or delay.
notes.explanation: The guidance calls it often the first major shift in production activity and the key to faster, more flexible production.
notes.example: Like a sandwich counter where bread, fillings and wrapping sit side by side, not in separate rooms.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – Cellular Manufacturing, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is load levelling?
notes.back: Working out the quantities and types of product needed each day to meet orders, then making them in a smooth daily sequence.
notes.explanation: The guidance says this lets a plant make varied products every day while keeping inventory and delay low.
notes.example: Like a school canteen planning each day’s quantities of each dish from the orders already placed.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is single-minute exchange of die (SMED)?
notes.back: A technique for converting a machine or process quickly so that it makes a different product.
notes.explanation: With quick changeovers, one cell and set of tools can make a variety of products and respond fast to changes in demand.
notes.example: Like a theatre crew changing the scenery between acts in seconds, rather than closing the show for an hour.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – Cellular Manufacturing, “Step 2: Converting to a Process-based Layout”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is poka-yoke?
notes.back: Mistake-proofing: simple fail-safe mechanisms that make mistakes impossible, or at least easy to detect and correct.
notes.explanation: The term joins the Japanese words for an inadvertent mistake and for prevent.
notes.example: Like a microwave that will not start while its door is open.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is autonomation?
notes.back: Transferring human intelligence to machines so that they can stop, start, load and unload automatically.
notes.explanation: Machines can often detect a defective part, stop and signal for help, which frees operators for other value-added work. The guidance also calls this jidoka, or ‘automation with a human touch’.
notes.example: Like a kettle that switches itself off when the water boils, so nobody has to stand and watch it.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – Cellular Manufacturing, “Step 2: Converting to a Process-based Layout”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is total productive maintenance (TPM)?
notes.back: An approach that engages all levels and functions of an organisation to get the most overall effectiveness from production equipment.
notes.explanation: Preventive maintenance traditionally sits in the maintenance department; this approach involves everyone from the plant floor to senior executives.
notes.example: Like a hospital where nurses, porters and managers all help keep the scanners working, not only the engineers.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is autonomous maintenance?
notes.back: Training operators to take care of the equipment and machines they work with, as a daily routine.
notes.explanation: The guidance calls it a key aspect of TPM: operators take a key role in preventive maintenance.
notes.example: Like drivers checking their own tyre pressure and oil each morning rather than leaving it to the garage.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is overall equipment effectiveness (OEE)?
notes.back: A TPM index of how effectively equipment is used, built from its availability, performance and product quality rate.
notes.explanation: The guidance names it as the measure behind TPM’s efficient-equipment technique, which starts by finding the losses holding performance back.
notes.example: Like a single fitness score for a machine that falls whenever it is stopped, running slowly or making rejects.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is standard work?
notes.back: The best sequence of activities for carrying out a given operation.
notes.explanation: Improvements made in rapid improvement events are written up as standard work so that staff understand and follow the new process consistently.
notes.example: Like a recipe card that fixes the order of steps so every cook makes the dish the same way.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Methods to Eliminate Waste in Everyday Activities”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a visual control?
notes.back: A display that reinforces standard procedures and shows an activity’s status, so every employee can see it and act.
notes.explanation: The Starter Kit says they are often set up during rapid improvement events to simplify work areas and give feedback on performance.
notes.example: Like a ward board that shows at a glance which beds are free and which are being cleaned.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Methods to Eliminate Waste in Everyday Activities”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Application forms keep arriving with boxes left blank and have to be sent back. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Defects.
notes.explanation: The Starter Kit’s examples of defects include errors in data or documents and missing information.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Staff compile a weekly report that nobody reads. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Overproduction.
notes.explanation: Producing reports, copies or work that nobody asked for is the Starter Kit’s picture of overproduction.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A case sits untouched for four days until a manager signs it off. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Waiting.
notes.explanation: Work held up for data, decisions, reviews or approvals is the Starter Kit’s example of waiting.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Experienced inspectors are never asked for ideas about the process they run every day. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Not utilising knowledge and skills.
notes.explanation: The Starter Kit’s examples include under-using employees’ skills, ideas and creativity, and a lack of teamwork.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A contract is carried between three buildings to collect signatures. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Transportation.
notes.explanation: Moving documents about when they need not move, such as routing them for signatures, is the Starter Kit’s example of transportation.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A backlog of 300 unprocessed claims builds up. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Inventory.
notes.explanation: The Starter Kit counts backlogs of work, surplus materials or information and obsolete files as inventory.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Clerks walk to another floor several times a day to fetch blank forms. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Motion.
notes.explanation: The Starter Kit lists people’s unnecessary movement to find files, data or supplies as motion.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Every routine request needs five approvals, though one would do. Which DOWNTIME waste is this?
notes.back: Excess processing.
notes.explanation: Needless process steps, rework and too many approvals are the Starter Kit’s examples of excess processing.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Process Wastes Targeted by Lean (DOWNTIME)”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which waste is in the eight-waste DOWNTIME list but not in LeanOhio’s list of seven wastes?
notes.back: Not utilising knowledge and skills.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio’s seven are transportation, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, over-processing and defects; the Environmental Professional’s Guide also counts seven.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “TIM WOOD”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In LeanOhio’s glossary, what do muda, mura and muri mean?
notes.back: Muda: waste. Mura: abnormality. Muri: stress or strain.
notes.explanation: Only muda is the Japanese term for waste itself; the glossary defines the other two as separate problems.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Muda”, “Mura”, “Muri”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which 5S step separates what a work area needs from what it does not, and removes the rest?
notes.back: Sort.
notes.explanation: The next step, set in order, then organises only what is left.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “5S”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After clearing out unused items, a team gives every remaining tool its own labelled, colour-coded place. Which 5S step is this?
notes.back: C) Set in order
notes.choices:
A) Sort
B) Shine
C) Set in order
D) Sustain
notes.choicesExplained: A: sort removes what is not needed, and that was already done. B: shine means cleaning and inspecting the area. D: sustain makes 5S a way of life; it does not arrange anything.
notes.explanation: Set in order organises what remains, and the guide says a typical 5S project results in tools and materials kept in labelled, colour-coded storage.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “5S”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which 5S step cleans and inspects the work area?
notes.back: Shine.
notes.explanation: The guide’s short gloss for this step links cleaning with solving problems.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “5S”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which 5S step makes cleaning, inspection and safety practices consistent?
notes.back: Standardise.
notes.explanation: The guide’s short gloss for this step is ‘make consistent’: everyone cleans, inspects and works safely in the same agreed way.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “5S”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which 5S step makes 5S a way of life?
notes.back: Sustain.
notes.explanation: The guide’s short gloss for this last step is keeping it up.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “5S”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the four steps of value stream mapping, what comes first?
notes.back: Identifying the product value stream to map.
notes.explanation: Only once the value stream is chosen does the team draw its current-state map in step two.
notes.source: NIST Manufacturing Extension Partnership, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Value stream mapping generally involves four steps: Identify the product value stream to map

notes.front: In the four steps of value stream mapping, what does step two produce?
notes.back: A current-state map of materials, processes and the flow of information.
notes.explanation: The map records information flow as well as the physical materials and processes.
notes.source: NIST Manufacturing Extension Partnership, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Develop the current state map of materials, processes and flow of information

notes.front: In value stream mapping, what does the step after drawing the current-state map involve?
notes.back: Diagnosing problems, identifying opportunities for improvement and defining a future state.
notes.explanation: The future state is defined only after the current state has been mapped and its problems diagnosed.
notes.source: NIST Manufacturing Extension Partnership, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Develop the current state map of materials, processes and flow of information Diagnose problems, identify opportunities for improvement and define a future state

notes.front: What is the fourth and last step of value stream mapping?
notes.back: Implementing improvements.
notes.explanation: Improvements come last, after a future state has been defined in step three.
notes.source: NIST Manufacturing Extension Partnership, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Diagnose problems, identify opportunities for improvement and define a future state Implement improvements

notes.front: What two maps does a value stream mapping event typically produce, and what does each show?
notes.back: A current-state map of the targeted process as it is, and a future-state map of the desired process flow.
notes.explanation: The guide says the event also produces an implementation plan for getting from the current state to the future state.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the lean guide, what do practitioners use value stream mapping to decide?
notes.back: Which lean implementation projects to prioritise and select, including where to aim future kaizen events.
notes.explanation: The maps highlight where waste arises, so they show which processes or steps are worth targeting.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to LeanOhio, how does a value stream map differ in level and span from a typical Six Sigma process map?
notes.back: It is higher-level (about 5–10 boxes) and broader, typically running from receipt of raw material to delivery of finished goods.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio adds that it gathers a broader range of information and is used to decide where to focus future projects and kaizen events.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Value Stream Mapping”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Permits take 90 days to issue, but nobody can say where the time goes across the five offices involved. Which tool should the team use first to see the whole flow?
notes.back: D) VSM
notes.choices:
A) 5S
B) SMED
C) Poka-yoke
D) VSM
notes.choicesExplained: A: 5S organises a single workspace; it does not show a flow across offices. B: SMED shortens changeovers, which are not the problem here. C: poka-yoke stops individual mistakes; it does not show where time goes.
notes.explanation: A value stream map gives a high-level picture of the whole flow and highlights non-value-added time, including work waiting in process.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Value Stream Mapping”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the lean guide, kaizen events are rapid process-improvement events lasting {{c1::2 to 5}} days.
notes.explanation: Chosen improvements are often in place within 72 hours of the start, usually without large capital spending.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Kaizen Events”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Staff from finance, purchasing and the warehouse spend four days on the invoicing process, try changes on the spot and have most in place by the end of the week, without buying equipment. What is this?
notes.back: A) A kaizen event
notes.choices:
A) A kaizen event
B) Autonomous maintenance
C) 5S
D) Load levelling
notes.choicesExplained: D: load levelling plans each day’s product quantities; it is not a team improvement event. B: autonomous maintenance is operators caring for their own equipment day to day. C: 5S organises and cleans a workspace; it does not redesign a process.
notes.explanation: A cross-functional team, a few days, rapid implementation and low capital spending are the marks of a kaizen event in the guide.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “Kaizen Events”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the lean guidance, what layout is typically a prerequisite for just-in-time production?
notes.back: A cellular production layout.
notes.explanation: JIT uses the cellular layout to cut inventory and work in process significantly.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does LeanOhio distinguish pull from push?
notes.back: Pull: made because the customer requested it. Push: made and delivered whether or not anyone asked for it.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio says pull gives a steady flow of production and delivery, while pushed work is simply dumped into the process.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Pull”, “Push”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a clinic store room each supply bin holds a card. When a bin empties, its card goes to the supplier, who sends exactly one bin’s worth. What is the card?
notes.back: B) A kanban
notes.choices:
A) A takt time
B) A kanban
C) A poka-yoke device
D) A value stream map
notes.choicesExplained: A: takt time is a pace, time per part, not a signal. C: poka-yoke devices prevent or flag mistakes. D: a value stream map is a picture of a whole flow, not a trigger to replenish.
notes.explanation: A kanban signals that more is needed from the previous step, so only what has been used is replaced: a pull system rather than push.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A planner says: “To meet customer orders, one finished unit must leave the line every 90 seconds.” Which term names that figure?
notes.back: D) Takt time
notes.choices:
A) Lead time
B) Throughput
C) OEE
D) Takt time
notes.choicesExplained: A: lead time is the time a supplier sets to meet a customer request, not a pace per part. B: throughput is a count of items per unit of time, not time per part. C: OEE is a percentage rating of equipment.
notes.explanation: A pace set by customer demand and given as time per part is exactly how the guidance defines takt time.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In LeanOhio’s glossary, what is lead time, and is it the same as cycle time?
notes.back: The time, set by the supplier, needed to meet a customer request or demand. It is not the same as cycle time.
notes.explanation: The glossary adds the warning to the definition itself; takt time, by contrast, is a pace set by customer demand.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Lead Time”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Rearranged, Little’s law gives: cycle time = items in process ÷ {{c1::throughput per unit of time}}.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam uses cycle time here for the average time each item spends in the process.
notes.source: MoreSteam, Little’s Law Calculator Tutorial
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A licensing team has 60 applications in process on average and completes 12 a day. By Little’s law, about how long does an application spend in the process?
notes.back: C) 5 days
notes.choices:
A) 0.2 days
B) 720 days
C) 5 days
D) 48 days
notes.choicesExplained: B: that multiplies the two figures, which gives items in process only when the known values are throughput and time. A: that divides throughput by items in process, the wrong way round. D: that subtracts the figures, which the law never does.
notes.explanation: Time in process equals items in process divided by throughput: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 days.
notes.source: MoreSteam, Little’s Law Calculator Tutorial
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does batch-and-queue production differ from one-piece flow?
notes.back: Batch and queue runs large lots that move on only when the whole batch is done; one-piece flow moves each item on singly.
notes.explanation: The guide describes lean as a shift from functionally aligned batch-and-queue mass production to product-aligned, one-piece flow pull production.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “How Lean Factories Differ from Traditional Manufacturing Environments”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a cellular layout, machines are usually placed in a {{c1::U or C}} shape, close together, with room for only a little work in process.
notes.explanation: The guidance says the shape reduces how far the operator has to move.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – Cellular Manufacturing, “Step 2: Converting to a Process-based Layout”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A plant moves its cutting, drilling and finishing machines side by side, so each part passes through all three before the next part starts. What has it adopted?
notes.back: A) Cellular manufacturing
notes.choices:
A) Cellular manufacturing
B) Batch and queue
C) Load levelling
D) TPM
notes.choicesExplained: B: batch and queue sends large lots between separate departments. C: load levelling plans daily quantities and mix; it does not rearrange machines. D: TPM is about keeping equipment effective, not about layout.
notes.explanation: Placing steps in sequence so single pieces flow through them with little transport or delay is what the guidance calls cellular manufacturing.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – Cellular Manufacturing, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Varying the mix of products made on a single line, to level production, is sometimes called {{c1::shish-kebab}} production.
notes.explanation: Spreading production evenly over time gives a smooth flow between processes, instead of making large runs of identical products to store.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – JIT/Kanban, “Introduction”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to MoreSteam, why does lean production need quick changeovers?
notes.back: Lean depends on small lots, and small lots depend on quick changeovers; long ones force large in-process inventories.
notes.explanation: Stock has to be held to keep production fed while a long changeover is under way.
notes.source: MoreSteam Toolbox, Quick Changeover (SMED)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In SMED, what is the difference between internal and external setup?
notes.back: Internal setup is changeover work done while the machine is stopped; external setup is preparation done while it is still running.
notes.explanation: When SMED was developed, almost all changeover work was done with the press stopped.
notes.source: MoreSteam Toolbox, Quick Changeover (SMED)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before a mould change, a technician fetches and preheats the next mould while the press is still running the current job. What kind of setup work is this?
notes.back: C) External setup
notes.choices:
A) Autonomous maintenance
B) Internal setup
C) External setup
D) Load levelling
notes.choicesExplained: B: internal setup is done while the machine is stopped, and this press is still running. A: autonomous maintenance is operators caring for their equipment, not preparing a changeover. D: load levelling sets daily quantities and mix.
notes.explanation: Work done while the machine runs is external; moving work there from the stopped time is how SMED shortens changeovers.
notes.source: MoreSteam Toolbox, Quick Changeover (SMED)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In MoreSteam’s account of SMED, what happens in the stages after the preliminary one, where all setup work is mixed together?
notes.back: Internal and external setup are separated; internal work is moved to external; then all elements are continually improved.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam links the last stage to kaizen: continual improvement of both internal and external work.
notes.source: MoreSteam Toolbox, Quick Changeover (SMED)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between a prevention and a detection poka-yoke device?
notes.back: A prevention device makes the mistake impossible; a detection device signals that a mistake has been made so it can be corrected quickly.
notes.explanation: These are the two major categories of poka-yoke device the guidance names; they differ in whether the error can happen at all.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A packing-line scale beeps when a sealed box weighs less than it should, so the packer can add the missing item. What is the scale?
notes.back: A) A detection device
notes.choices:
A) A detection device
B) A kanban
C) Autonomation
D) A prevention device
notes.choicesExplained: D: a prevention device would make the short box impossible to pack; here the mistake happens and is then flagged. B: a kanban signals a need for more parts, not an error. C: autonomation is a machine stopping itself; here a person is alerted to fix the box.
notes.explanation: A detection device tells the user a mistake has been made so it can be corrected quickly.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Toyota Production System “house”, what are the two pillars?
notes.back: Just-in-time production and jidoka (built-in quality).
notes.explanation: The roof is the customer goal of top quality at lowest cost with the shortest lead time; the foundation is standardisation. Jidoka is the Japanese name for autonomation: equipment that stops itself and signals when a problem occurs.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional’s Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 2: What Is Lean?, “History of Lean Activity”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the TPM table of major losses, which loss is downtime for repairs after unexpected equipment failure?
notes.back: Unexpected breakdown losses.
notes.explanation: Its costs include lost production, labour and spare parts.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the TPM table of major losses, which loss is production lost during product changeovers, shift changes or other changes in operating conditions?
notes.back: Set-up and adjustment losses.
notes.explanation: Its cost is the production opportunity, or yield, lost while operating conditions are being changed.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the TPM table of major losses, which loss is frequent downtime of zero to 10 minutes that is hard to record by hand?
notes.back: Stoppage losses.
notes.explanation: Because they are hard to record, these losses usually stay hidden from efficiency reports.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the TPM table of major losses, which loss comes from running equipment more slowly to avoid quality defects or minor stoppages?
notes.back: Speed losses.
notes.explanation: It usually goes unrecorded, because the equipment keeps running.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the TPM table of major losses, which loss is off-specification output, caused by equipment malfunction, that must be reworked or scrapped?
notes.back: Quality defect losses.
notes.explanation: Here an equipment problem turns straight into rework or scrap.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the TPM table of major losses, which loss is wear and tear that shortens equipment’s productive life and forces earlier replacement?
notes.back: Equipment and capital investment losses.
notes.explanation: Its cost is more frequent capital spending on replacement equipment.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The lean TPM guidance speaks of five major losses in its text. How many does its table of major losses list?
notes.back: Six. This deck follows the table.
notes.explanation: The table’s sixth entry is equipment and capital investment losses, from wear that shortens equipment life.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A labelling machine jams for two or three minutes several times a shift; operators clear it and nothing is logged. Which major equipment loss is this?
notes.back: D) Stoppage losses
notes.choices:
A) Unexpected breakdown losses
B) Speed losses
C) Quality defect losses
D) Stoppage losses
notes.choicesExplained: A: breakdown losses are failures needing repair, not brief jams cleared on the spot. B: speed losses come from running slower, not from stopping. C: quality defect losses are off-specification output, not lost time.
notes.explanation: Frequent stops of up to 10 minutes that are hard to record by hand are the guidance’s stoppage losses.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”, table of major losses
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: OEE is calculated by {{c1::multiplying}} equipment availability, performance and product quality rate, each as a percentage.
notes.explanation: The guidance says that with these figures a plant can see how much time goes to each major loss, and where to focus.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A line has availability 90%, performance 95% and quality rate 99%. What is its OEE, to one decimal place?
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the average of the three, but OEE multiplies them. C: that is only the lowest factor. D: that is only the highest factor.
notes.explanation: 0.90 × 0.95 × 0.99 = 0.846, so every shortfall in any one factor pulls the total down.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean Thinking and Methods – TPM, “Method and Implementation Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In LeanOhio’s glossary, how does standard work handle the work it describes?
notes.back: It breaks the work into elements that are sequenced, organised and repeatedly followed.
notes.explanation: The aim is the most efficient way to make a product or deliver a service at a balanced flow and a desired output rate.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Standard Work”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two things LeanOhio includes in a visual control system?
notes.back: Signs and colour-coding; others include information displays, layouts and mistake-proofing devices.
notes.explanation: The glossary says such a system makes flow, standards, schedules and problems obvious even to a casual observer.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Visual Controls”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Above each workstation a board shows the day’s target, the count so far and a red card when work is stuck, so anyone passing can see the status. What is this?
notes.back: B) A visual control
notes.choices:
A) Standard work
B) A visual control
C) A value stream map
D) Load levelling
notes.choicesExplained: A: standard work is the set sequence of activities for an operation, not a status display. C: a value stream map pictures a whole flow for planning, not live status. D: load levelling plans daily quantities.
notes.explanation: Showing an activity’s status so every employee can see it and act is what a visual control does.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit, Version 4.0, Chapter 2, “Methods to Eliminate Waste in Everyday Activities”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
